title: GT17-670GD - EVOLVED OPERATIONAL USER INTERFACES (EXPRO+)
description: Existing operational user interfaces for ground segment are primarily built on aging software platforms characterized by deprecated technologies, a monolithic architecture and rigid implementation. While these legacy platforms provide stability for established scenarios, it struggles to adapt to modern operational demands specifically the introduction of remote operations, cloud infrastructure management, and the seamless integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Building on the EGS-CC WebUI and the PulseUI, a specialized WebUI branch tailored for operational environments, the new approach has enabled support for comprehensive UI testing, facilitate remote control capabilities, and better align with the microservices architecture backends. To overcome these challenges and achieve the goals of the project, an architectural and design approach based on the following will be required: - Web-Based Architecture: To guarantee high flexibility and stability. - Unified Design System: Establishing a common look and feel across the ground segment.  - Industry-Standard Framework Principles: Adopting the principles of established UI frameworks (such as Material Design). This will provide a comprehensive suite of reusable components, complete with intuitive documentation and tutorials, hence mitigates the risk of "technology islands".

title: AI ASSISTED SYSML V2 SPACE MODEL INTERACTION AND KNOWLEDGE REUSE - EXPRO+
description: Objective:To develop and validate an AI-based assistant for interactive access, querying and assisted manipulation of SysML v2 space system models to reduce modelling effort and increase design quality.Description:Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) is an approach to manage the complexity of future space systems.Working effectively with large digital models is challenging; understanding structure and dependencies,reusing assets across projects, and extracting decision-relevant information is time-consuming andexpert-dependent.Limited and non-intuitive access to very large models slows MBSE adoption and reduces the return oninvestments, especially in early phases where it drives duplication, and late inconsistency discovery causeshigher design risk. SysML v2 introduces combined textual and graphical modelling with a standardised API for programmatic access, which lowers the access barrier. AI - and particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) - can help translate user intent into controlled, explainable interactions with these formal SysML v2 models, overcoming the barriers identified.This activity will develop an AI assistant that acts as an intermediate layer between users and formal modelsand operates exclusively via the SysML v2 textual notation and standard API. It will support (i) natural-language assistance for incremental model creation and modification, (ii) model querying and automated consistency checking, (iii) guided exploration of dependencies, (iv) identification and extraction of reusable model elements, and (v) structured summarization of model content for expert and non-expert stakeholders. The focus is on human assistance, incremental model generation and knowledge exploitation that helps system engineerswork with large system models - not on autonomous end-to-end model generation or mission-specifictoolchains.This activity encompasses the following tasks:- Review of SysML v2 capabilities, APIs, and relevant AI techniques for model creation and interaction- Identification of representative use cases for querying, exploration, and reuse of SysML v2 models- Definition of a reference architecture ensuring controlled AI interaction via the SysML v2 API- Development of proof-of-concept AI components for model generation, querying and summarization- Validation of the approach on representative SysML v2 models, using the ESA MBSE methodology- Assessment of benefits, limitations, and roadmap towards higher TRL.The activity will result in validated concepts, software prototypes, and documented lessons learned, enablingfollow-on developments under GSTP or other programmes focusing on operational deployment.Software shall be delivered under an ESA Software Community License, so that any individuals or entitieswithin ESA Member States can access it and can provide update to the community of users.

title: DISTRIBUTED TEMPERATURE AND STRAIN USING FIBRE OPTICS FOR THE CHARACTERISATION OF LARGE ANTENNA STRUCTURES - EXPRO PLUS
description: Large spaceborne antennas are increasingly required to provide large apertures while meeting stringent mass, dimensional stability and RF performance requirements. Examples include large active phased-array SAR antennas, reflectarrays and deployable reflector antennas. Thermally induced distortions, mechanical loads, deployment effects and long-term structural variations can result in changesof the antenna geometry which may affect the antenna RF characteristics.The knowledge of the actual antenna geometry and its evolution in orbit can therefore provide valuable information for the characterisation and prediction of antenna performance. Conventional temperature sensors provide measurements at discrete locations and do not directly provide information on structural strain or deformation. Similarly, direct geometrical metrology of large antenna structures may require dedicated instrumentation and may be difficult to implement in orbit.Fibre-optic sensing technologies offer the possibility of obtaining quasi-distributed (e.g. Fibre BraggGratings, Fabry-Perot)  and distributed (e.g. Rayleigh, Brillouin and Raman scattering) measurements over large structures with lowsensor mass and limited electrical harnessing. However, their application to large spaceborne antenna structures requires addressing several aspects, including temperature-strain discrimination, sensor integration and routing, spatial resolution, environmental compatibility and reconstruction of the structural deformation from the measured quantities.Previous work has demonstrated the use of fibre-optic strain measurements for shape reconstruction of large and deployable structures and antenna elements. In parallel, experience from large SAR antennas, such as Sentinel-1 and ROSE-L, shows the importance of accurate antenna-pattern knowledge and of accounting for antenna-pattern variations in instrument calibration and data processing.The present activity aims at connecting these two areas by investigating whether distributed/quasi-distributed fibre-optic measurements can provide sufficiently accurate knowledge of the thermomechanical state and deformation of a large antenna structure to support antenna characterisation and, potentially,antenna-pattern prediction or correction.The objective of this activity is to investigate, develop and experimentally validate afibre-optic sensing system for distributed temperature and strain monitoring of large spaceborne antenna structures.The activity shallassess fibre-optic sensing techniques capable of providing distributed measurements of temperature and mechanical strain and shall investigate methods for separating the two measurands.Methods to reconstruct the thermomechanical deformation of the antenna structure from the fibre-optic measurements shall be developed and validated. The impact of the reconstructed structural deformationontheantenna RF performance shall be assessed, including the feasibility of using the reconstructed structural state for antenna-patternprediction and compensation.A representative breadboard shall be designed, manufactured and tested under representative mechanical and thermal loading conditions.

title: COMPATIBILITY VALIDATION TESTBED OF THE OPTICAL HEAD AND ITS CONTROL OF OPTICAL COMMUNICATION TERMINALS (ARTES 4.0 SL SPL 5H.015)
description: Objective: The objective of this activity is to develop a testbed that will test the interoperability between different suppliers of optical communication terminals. Thisshall include free-space optics testing to evaluate the pointing, acquisition, and tracking performance.TargetedImprovements:To enable independent on-ground validation of optical communication terminal interoperability ina facility located in ESA member states.Description: With an increasing number of constellations considering the use of optical inter satellite links and cross-atmospheric links, it is important to test, validateand ultimately certify the interoperability between different laser terminals manufactured by multiple suppliers.This activity will develop the capability of enabling independent interoperability validation between various laser communication terminals. The focus willbe on pointing, acquisition and tracking performance validation for both intersatellite and cross-atmospheric optical links. The developed testbed shallenable the performancevalidation of the terminal optical head in free space, and the compatibility validation of the pointing, acquisition and trackingsequence implemented by optical terminal (both space and ground) suppliers. The testbed will enable the validation to be carried out between two terminalsunder test from different suppliers and shall be accessible to all the ESA member states industries.Procurement Policy: C(1) = Activity restricted to non-prime contractors (incl. SMEs).
